description: Facebook was just the victim of the largest hack in its history, your account may have been impacted. Criminals are spreading a fake tech support scam, but we'll tell you how to avoid it. You might be shocked to learn just how unsecure U.S. elections actually are. All that and more in Tech News Today from Komando.com.

asr.full_text: Welcome to Tech News Today, a podcast about keeping you informed and empowered by giving. You the latest tech stories that impact your daily life. It's Monday, October 1st, and I'm. Spike Spangle. Coming up in a bit, we'll tell you how to protect your Facebook account after the. Biggest hack in its history. Plus, there's another tech support scam making the rounds to watch for,. And you might be shocked to learn just how unsecure U.S. elections actually are. All that and more in Tech News Today from Commando.com. We start with the gory details of the biggest hack in the history of Facebook. According to the social media giant, hackers were able to exploit part of its. Code that let them take over accounts. They did it by stealing access tokens,. Which are used to keep people logged into their accounts over long periods of. Time without needing to re-enter passwords. The bad guys gained access to. Nearly 50 million accounts. An additional 40 million were potentially impacted, so. Facebook reset the tokens for all 90 million accounts. That means if you try. Checking Facebook over the weekend as I did and were forced to re-enter your. Password as I was, you were part of this breach. If so, once you log back in you'll. See a banner at the top of your newsfeed that says an important security update. There's also a link that you can click to see details of what happened. Since it. Was access tokens that the hackers stole Facebook said you don't need to change. Your password, but I wouldn't trust that. We recommend changing your password as soon as. Possible. Also, you should set up two-factor authentication for your Facebook account. That means anytime you or a hacker tries logging into your account, you'll receive a special code. Through text or email. That way, you'll enter it and you can successfully get in. There are more. Security precautions that you can take to make your account safer. To learn more, go to commando.com. And search for our story titled, What to Do Now Because of the Facebook Hack. Cybercriminals have been busy lately. One of their latest schemes is circulating another tech support scam. Victims of the hoax are being redirected to websites through malicious advertisements. The sites are built to display a pop-up message that looks like a Microsoft notification saying your computer is infected with malware. The message contains a phone number that you're supposed to call to get rid of the infection. The problem is, it's a scam. If you call the number, you'll be speaking with crooks who ask you for your credit card. To pay for their help getting rid of the malware. Don't fall for it. Another problem is the popup itself. It won't go away. But don't worry, it's pretty easy to remove it yourself. Just click on the Windows search box in the lower left corner and search for Task Manager. Then open Task Manager and right click on the browser you have opened, listed under. The Processes tab, and click End. If you've got multiple tabs open, repeat this step for each tab. That's it, you're done. That wasn't so bad, was it? We have more tech news ahead,. But now a quick thank you to our amazing partners. At Casper Sleep. Wouldn't it be nice to trust the election process 100%? Unfortunately, with all the reports. Of foreign government meddling. And all the fake political news circulating on social media,. It's almost impossible these days. But things are even worse than you thought. It turns out that there is disturbing security flaws. Our voting machines. And get this, it's been known for nearly 11 years and nothing is being done. About it. The vulnerability was found in high-speed ballot scanners called the M650. The manufacturer. Stopped making them a decade ago but are still in 23 states across the country. Security researchers. Say they can be infected with malware with the help of a removable zip drive. If the scanner is. Hacked, it could change the outcome of an election, which raises the question, why aren't we voting. From encrypted websites yet. Hmm, I have a theory. Have you ever captured that perfect selfie? You know, the one in an exotic location at just the right moment? More and more people are doing this, and they're taking huge risks by going to dangerous locations. You won't believe just how dangerous some of them really are. A new report shows that an average of 43 people per year have died while taking selfies since. 2011. The most common causes of selfie deaths are drowning, being hit by a vehicle, and suffering. A fall. A group of people called Millennial Daredevils account for nearly half of all the selfie. Deaths, and most of them are male. You can find horrifying footage on YouTube of some of these daredevils climbing skyscrapers. To the top, just to take a selfie. And all this in the name of likes and swipes. It's become such a problem that popular tourist spots in India are implementing selfie. Bans. Researchers of this scary phenomenon are recommending that more restrictions be put in place around. The globe. Which is probably a good idea. Some people just need to be saved from themselves. Supposed to. We love a good breaking story here at Commando as well. But you never hear about products being leaked in person. Until now. According to Android Police, a Best Buy customer was able to purchase the latest model of Google's. Chromecast last week. The problem is, Google hasn't even held its annual Fall Hardware event announcing details. Of its new gadgets. That is scheduled for October 9th. We've been expecting a new version of Chromecast, since its technology is outdated. Its last upgrade was three years ago, but that speculation is now being confirmed. The lucky person who bought it immediately posted pictures of the third-generation Chromecast. On social media. I guess shopping old school brick and mortar stores sometimes pays off. Have you been paying attention to Apple's newest gadgets? One is an updated Apple Watch. It's the Series 4 and comes with a new feature that will contact emergency services for you. If you take a nasty fall. It sounds like a great way to get the help you need if you're incapacitated and can't. Call 911 yourself. But some people are worried that it's a terrible breach of privacy. It's mainly an opt-in service, meaning you have to opt in for it to work. However, Apple said that it's automatically enabled for users who enter their age as 65. Or older. This has raised privacy concerns for some attorneys and law professors around the country. That's because if the feature is automatically turned on and the Apple Watch mistakenly calls. 911, police would be able to enter your home without a warrant. One professor posted on social media that the Fourth Amendment Community Caretaking. Exception means police can enter your home without a warrant in plain view means they can. Seize contraband or other evidence of a crime. As usual, technology is usually faster than the laws. Here's a fun story from the developers at Google. They've hidden an easter egg within Google Search. It's a tribute to the classic text adventure games where players complete tasks simply by. Typing basic commands. If you want to check it out, type text adventure in a Google search. When you get to the search results page, right-click in the search box and click Inspect. A menu will appear on the right side of your screen. Click on the console tab at the top. You should see a giant capital G, part of the Google logo. The goal of the game is to find the rest of the letters making up the Google logo. Not quite as high-tech as Fortnite, but beats a night of Scrabble. By the way, once you're done listening to our podcast,. Do us a favor and give us a good rating on wherever you're listening to us. Write a few nice words so others can find our podcast more easily. We'd really appreciate it. And finally for today's Commando Kicker. During the Great Depression, you might not have realized that the Hoover Dam,. Then called the Boulder Dam, was responsible for over 100 deaths during its construction. But in a massive construction site, how do you get rid of the bodies of your co-workers? Well, in Chicago, it was cement shoes. But rumors had it that the easiest way was to just throw them in with the concrete,. Forever to be entombed within the dam. But a body isn't good for the integrity of concrete. So workers made sure that no one was left to spend eternity in the dam. The folks at Law & Order would be pleased to know. For more fun and interesting facts, go to commando.com and search for Commando Kicker. Well, that's our tech news today from commando.com. And special thanks to our partners at Capterra.

textual.observation: The source describes a tech-support scheme in which malicious advertisements redirect victims to websites displaying a fake Microsoft notification claiming that the computer is infected with malware; the notification provides a phone number to call, and callers are asked for a credit card payment for assistance.

evidence.quote: Victims of the hoax are being redirected to websites through malicious advertisements.
The sites are built to display a pop-up message that looks like a Microsoft notification saying your computer is infected with malware.
The message contains a phone number that you're supposed to call to get rid of the infection.
If you call the number, you'll be speaking with crooks who ask you for your credit card. To pay for their help getting rid of the malware.

textual.context: Presented as a news report and warning about a tech-support scam, not as a promotion; the source explicitly says the notification is a scam and advises viewers not to follow it.
textual.potential_relevance: The claimed malware infection and Microsoft-like notification are linked to a requested phone call and credit-card payment for remediation, describing a concrete support-scam mechanism for later context assessment.
textual.limitations: These records do not independently verify the websites, phone number, Microsoft affiliation, malware status, payment request, or any resulting transaction or loss.

textual_context_notes.observation: The program frames the described tech-support scheme as something viewers should avoid.

evidence.quote: Criminals are spreading a fake tech support scam, but we'll tell you how to avoid it.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as an informational technology news podcast covering multiple stories. Its tech-support-scam segment reports on criminals using fake Microsoft-like malware pop-ups, a phone number, and a credit-card request, while advising listeners not to fall for the scheme and explaining that the pop-up can be removed by the user.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The primary context is a warning about a third-party tech-support scam, including the reported fake notification, phone call, credit-card request, and advice not to follow it.

evidence.quote: Welcome to Tech News Today, a podcast about keeping you informed and empowered by giving.

evidence.observation: The speaker presents the tech-support scheme as conduct by cybercriminals and reports it as a scam.
evidence.quote: Cybercriminals have been busy lately. One of their latest schemes is circulating another tech support scam.

evidence.observation: The reported scheme uses a pop-up presented as resembling a Microsoft notification and claiming malware infection.
evidence.quote: The sites are built to display a pop-up message that looks like a Microsoft notification saying your computer is infected with malware.

evidence.observation: The reported pop-up directs the recipient to call a phone number for purported infection removal.
evidence.quote: The message contains a phone number that you're supposed to call to get rid of the infection.

evidence.observation: The report says the depicted actors request a credit card payment for purported malware-removal help.
evidence.quote: If you call the number, you'll be speaking with crooks who ask you for your credit card. To pay for their help getting rid of the malware.
